title: Effect of oxygen plasma treatment on the structural and superconducting properties of atomic-layer-deposited NbN thin films
authors: Nitesh Yerra, Mustafa Teke, Felix Otto, Marco Diegel, Detlef Born, Uwe Hübner, Nan Du, Mario Ziegler, Sahitya Varma Vegesna, Heidemarie Krüger
abstract: Surface oxidation is a common concern for ultrathin NbN superconducting devices, yet which superconducting properties it affects has not been established for films grown by plasma-enhanced atomic layer deposition. We expose NbN films about 11.4 nm thick to an O$_2$ plasma for 0 to 60 s, which oxidizes the surface without etching the film, and characterize the same sample series by X-ray diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and transport measurements on 500 nm wide nanowires. XPS of the surface and the underlying layer shows that the plasma converts the surface to Nb$_2$O$_5$, whereas the bulk of the treated film is chemically identical to that of the untreated film. Crystalline $δ$-NbN remains intact. During exposure, the total film thickness rises and saturates between 40 and 60 s, indicating self-limiting surface oxide growth. The normal-state resistivity rises by 21% (dc) and 25% (optical) with the plasma dose, while the critical temperature and transition width are unchanged. The switching current densities of 4.9-6.2 MA/cm$^2$ at 4.2 K show no systematic dependence on the plasma dose. Their temperature dependence follows the dirty-limit depairing current of Kupriyanov and Lukichev, and the extrapolated switching currents reach 39-46% of the depairing current calculated from the optical resistivity and diffusion coefficient, in agreement with the width dependence reported for nanowires from the same process. The oxygen signature is confined to temperatures near $T_c$, where the supercurrent of the treated wires vanishes at least 0.5 K earlier than that of the untreated wire, consistent with a partially oxidized surface layer that acts on the film by the proximity effect. At these doses, oxygen narrows the temperature range of the supercurrent from above but does not systematically reduce the low-temperature current-carrying capacity of the wires.
summary: This work systematically investigates how controlled oxygen plasma oxidation affects superconducting $	ext{NbN}$ thin films. Using a combination of structural, chemical, and electrical measurements, the authors demonstrate that surface oxidation forms a stable oxide layer that primarily affects the supercurrent near the critical temperature via the proximity effect, leaving the core superconducting properties largely intact at lower temperatures.
main_problem: The study investigates how controlled surface oxidation of atomic-layer-deposited Niobium Nitride (NbN) thin films affects their structural integrity and superconducting properties.
main_result: Surface oxidation to $	ext{Nb}_2	ext{O}_5$ occurs, increasing normal-state resistivity but leaving the bulk crystalline $\delta$-NbN intact. This oxidation narrows the supercurrent temperature range near $T_c$ via the proximity effect without significantly reducing low-temperature current capacity.
method: The researchers used controlled $	ext{O}_2$ plasma treatment on $	ext{NbN}$ films, followed by comprehensive characterization using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and transport measurements on nanowires.
model_or_system: The physical system is ultrathin, superconducting $	ext{NbN}$ films patterned into nanowires. The analysis incorporates the proximity effect, modeling the surface oxide layer as a weakly superconducting or normal metal that interacts with the bulk superconductor.
key_observables: Surface oxidation state ($	ext{Nb}_2	ext{O}_5$), normal-state resistivity (dc and optical), critical temperature ($T_c$), transition width ($\Delta T_c$), and temperature dependence of supercurrent.
important_parameters: Plasma dose (0 to 60 s), nanowire width ($500 	ext{ nm}$), and temperature range near $T_c$.
main_assumptions: The surface oxidation is self-limiting, and the superconducting degradation near $T_c$ is primarily governed by the proximity effect from the surface oxide layer.
figures_summary: The notes indicate measurements of structural changes (XRD), chemical changes (XPS comparing surface vs. bulk), and electrical transport curves ($R(T)$ and $I_c(T)$) showing the temperature-dependent suppression of supercurrent.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of problem definition (surface oxidation concern), methodology (ALD growth, plasma treatment, multi-modal characterization), results presentation (structural, compositional, and electrical findings), and a theoretical interpretation based on the proximity effect.
why_interesting: While focused on superconductivity, the study of surface degradation and the proximity effect in ultrathin films touches upon concepts relevant to open quantum systems and decoherence, where surface interactions dictate bulk quantum behavior.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Background-subtracted GIXRD patterns of δ-NbN thin films exposed to O2 plasma for 0, 20, 40, and 60 s (sam- ples A_0s, B_20s, C_40s, and D_60s). The diffraction peaks correspond to the (111), (020), (022), and (131) reflections of cubic NbN. The raw GIXRD intensities were background- subtracted using a baseline fitted manually in the Malvern Panalytical HighScore Plus 4.9 powder diffraction software, smoothed with a Savitzky-Golay filter, and shown on a com- mon arbitrary intensity scale (arb. units). Only the range of 30◦–80◦is shown as a zoomed view, since the region below is dominated by the substrate signal.

FIG. 2. Background-subtracted XPS core-level spectra of the samples before and after sputtering, with gridlines added for direct intensity comparison. Top row, surface analysis (as-received): (a) Nb 3d, (b) C 1s, (c) N 1s, (d) O 1s. Bottom row, center-of-film analysis (after 15 min Ar+ sputtering): (e) Nb 3d, (f) C 1s, (g) N 1s, (h) O 1s. Blue: A_0s; red: D_60s. Dotted vertical lines mark the reference binding energies of the assigned components. In the Nb 3d panels the green lines are the 3d5/2 lines of NbN (204.1 eV), NbC (204.6 eV), Nb2N2−yO3+y (207.4 eV), and Nb2O5 (208.0 eV), and the black lines are the corresponding 3d3/2 partners, displaced by the spin-orbit splitting of 2.7 eV and...
